clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1992
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Gordon's stroke in June 1991, within the next year: your wrist injury stopped your playing in October, anxiety and functioning fell; you and Rafe clashed and he moved out in November; you were on your own getting high and absorbed in fixing radios by late November; by January 1992 you were lost and low, unable to get going, with no footing once he was gone and your mother about to remarry. Your late nights had picked up in secondary school, and you dropped chess and debate partway through; you liked late nights in 1989, unsure whether that was out of the ordinary. Your grandmother Winifred had a thyroid tumour treated within a year or so of being widowed, also a blow. These months held shifts in anxiety, functioning and relationship moves passing from one to the next; by the spring you were earning money fixing radios, and by early 1992 things looked to be settling, though the bleak year at community college followed later that autumn.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's bowel cancer diagnosis, 2001–2003
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Winifred found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, alongside your burnout and disastrous audition: from September 2001 you were running out of steam for performing, anxiety up and functioning falling by the month; in early 2002 came the audition, a near-total blank on family life for you across those years. By September 2002 you were on poor terms with family and friends, distance from your parents; you left Thornbury for Gull Harbour. You met Marisol at a winter party in early 2003, left Gull Harbour to live with her by June, and split within the year by October. Once you split, you sank into a deep depression that winter, symptom and functioning both down; you could not face your family, anxiety up and distance from your parents, though you relied gingerly on friends. Winifred spent her final months in your mother's home as the depression took hold. The shifts pile up close together from September 2001 onward, each one near another's, and settle once you returned to Thornbury and began work with your therapist in January 2004.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Lorna's death in January 2008, within months: you spent four weeks building with Silas at Alder Creek in July, and were too drained for conversation, distance from your mother; you left for nursing school in September and stopped speaking to her; the silence held for roughly a year. The shifts are yours alone—anxiety and relationship moves—and sit beside the loss of your grandmother and your move away from home.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, within the next two and a half years: you saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along, away from her by the wedding; your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in October 2017, symptom up. Your job steadied and paid well by June 2019, anxiety down, but by October you were constantly feeling you ought to drive projects forward, anxiety up; you started a sleeping pill that month. Your aunt Imogen's memory was slipping worse, and she lashes out when muddled, symptom and conflict up with her son Hal; your mother had a heart check-up after her siblings' illnesses. Your sister Tara's first child was due later in the autumn. In late October 2019, Wren was swamped—one thing after another—symptom, anxiety and functioning all down; you were too strict laying out a plan to settle her, overfunctioning; she talks with her father and brother all day, fusion among them. She settled once the weekend had a plan; the dinner went well, anxiety down and functioning up. But at the lake house that night you awoke from the small hours with no more sleep, symptom and anxiety up, and could only pull back as the others rose, distance; you felt you didn't belong. She was anxious when you'd had no sleep at family occasions, and there were long quiet drives home afterward. The shifts from October onward belong together: one person's swamped state, overfunctioning on your part, fusion in her family, and then your sleep breaking down at her family gathering. Things remain unsettled.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
